chapter_theme: Old friendship as the freedom to take liberties with each other. It teaches welcoming what a friend presumes to do, reading hurt charitably, and staying even through harm the friend causes.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar: what it is (801), the value of its liberty (802-803), welcoming what is done unasked (804), reading harm charitably (805), not leaving through harm (806-807), bearing faults (808), and what it earns (809-810).

801.reading: What is called old friendship? It is friendship that in no way cuts down the liberties that intimacy gives.
801.nuance: The definition is not about time, and Parimelazhagar says so outright. His list of permitted liberties is concrete: acting without asking, even acting to one's harm, taking what one needs, showing neither deference nor fear.

802.reading: Intimate liberty is a limb of friendship, and being as salt to it is the duty of the worthy.
802.nuance: உப்பு: the worthy person doesn't merely tolerate liberties but gives them savour. Manakkudavar gives a homely comparison: a bitter gourd stays bitter however much seasoning goes in, so without consent no sweetness comes.

803.reading: What use is long-practised friendship if one does not accept a friend's liberty as if one had done it oneself?
803.nuance: செய்தாங்கு is the core: treat the act as your own. Parimelazhagar adds that this holds even for what one wouldn't agree to, which is where the test really lies.

804.reading: When friends act unasked out of intimacy, those who are wise welcome it for how desirable it is.

positions.position: The act is one's own business done for one by a friend unasked, and nothing is better than finding it done.
positions.quote: ஒருவர்க்குத் தம் கருமம் தாம் அறியாமல் முடிந்திருத்தலின் ஊங்கு நன்மை யின்மையின்

positions.position: The act is something one doesn't approve, and one should still welcome it and not only permit it.

805.reading: If friends do something that hurts, understand it as either folly or great intimacy.
805.nuance: The verse is a rule of interpretation: two readings are allowed, and lack of love isn't one of them. Parimelazhagar brings in fate, saying the folly comes from a fate of loss. The verse does not. Pope's 'not only... but also' blurs the either-or that the commentators find.

806.reading: Those who hold to the bounds will not give up the bond of those who stand in old friendship, even when ruin comes.
806.nuance: For Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar the ruin comes from that friend, which makes this harder than loyalty in hard times. The verse's தொலைவிடத்தும் doesn't itself say who caused the ruin.

807.reading: Even when destructive things are done to them, those whose bond has come by the way of love do not cut off love.
807.nuance: The verse does not say the friendship goes unaltered in every way, only that அன்பு does not end. It locates the constancy in love and not in the deeds.

808.reading: For those who have the strength of intimacy not to listen to reports of a friend's lapse, the day the friend lapses has its own meaning.
808.nuance: The verse has a sting: the lapse is what reveals the strength. Parimelazhagar says the bond only shows when it is tested, so other days don't count.

positions.position: The day a friend lapses is a day of real worth, for it alone shows such intimacy.
positions.quote: செய்து போந்துழியல்லது அவ்வுரிமை வெளிப்படாமையின், செய்யாதன நாளல்லவாயின.

positions.position: Such a day is a good day.
positions.quote: நட்டோர் தப்புச் செய்யின், அந்த நாள் நல்ல நாளாம்

positions.position: The reverse: if they do wrong to one so trusting, all the days of that friendship were wasted.

809.reading: The world loves those who do not give up the friendship of friends whose bond has come down unbroken.
809.nuance: Parimelazhagar gives a motive: everyone reasons that such a person would be like this to them too, and comes to seek friendship. Loyalty to one is an advertisement to all. Manakkudavar's வழிவந்த points rather to friendship inherited through family.

810.reading: Those who do not depart from their nature toward old friends are wanted even by those who do not want them.
810.nuance: The commentators take விழையார் as enemies. The verse's own word is softer, 'those who don't desire', and the tight wordplay விழையார் விழையப் works without naming any foe.

links.note: Salt in both, and both about intimacy that hurts a little. In 802 the worthy are salt to friendship's liberties, and in 1302 lovers' sulking is salt that spoils when overdone. 1302 supplies the measure 802 leaves out.

797 says dropping a fool's friendship is gain. 805 says when an old friend hurts you, consider it folly and go on. The same பேதைமை is a reason for leaving in one chapter and an excuse for staying in the next, and the only difference is how old the bond is.

800 says pay if you must to escape a bad friend. 807 says love does not end even when an old friend ruins you. Between them lies a question the Kural doesn't settle: at what point does a harmful friend stop being an old friend and become one you never should have made?

source_issues: 809: Manakkudavar's entry opens with a fragment of the verse and ends with a stray '9'.
